segs: Seven IAM interview questions you need
to master. You finally landed the
interview. Your resume got noticed, the
recruiter liked your background, and
you're one interview away from getting a
role in identity and access management.
But, there's a problem. Most people
prepare the wrong way. They spend hours
memorizing definitions and studying
certifications only to get blindsided by
questions they weren't expecting. The
truth is, IAM interviews are
surprisingly repetitive. Hiring managers
tend to ask the same core questions over
and over again. So, in this video, I'm
going to walk you through seven IAM
questions
>> [music]
>> you absolutely need to master if you
want to land an IAM job in 2026. Let's
get into it. Question one, what is
identity and access management? This
sounds like an easy question, but a lot
of candidates over complicate it. A
strong answer might sound like this.
Identity and access management, or IAM,
is the process of ensuring that the
right type of people have the access to
the right resources at the right time.
IAM teams manage user identities,
authentication, authorization, and
access through the entire employee life
cycle. Keep it simple. The interviewer
isn't looking for a textbook definition.
They want to know whether you actually
understand the process of IAM. Question
two, can you explain the difference
between authentication and
authorization? This is one of the most
common IAM questions. Here's the easiest
way to remember it. Authentication
answers the question of who are you?
Examples, passwords, MFA, biometrics,
security keys. Authorization answers the
question, what are you allowed to do?
Examples, permissions,
RBAC, roles, access policies. Think of
it this way. Authentication gets you in
the building. Authorization determines
which rooms you can enter. Question
three, what is RBAC? RBAC stands for
role-based access control. Instead of
assigning permissions to every employee
individually, companies create roles.
For example, HR employees get HR
permissions, finance employees get
finance permissions, managers [music]
get additional access. RBAC improves
security, simplifies management, and
helps enforce the principle of least
privilege. A lot of interviewers will
follow it up with, "Why is RBAC
important?" Be prepared to explain that
it reduces administrative overhead and
lowers the risk of excessive access.
Question four, "Can you explain single
sign on and MFA?" You will almost
certainly be asked this question. Single
sign on allows users to authenticate
once and access multiple applications.
Multi-factor authentication requires
users to verify identity using multiple
methods. Examples of this include
passwords plus phone notification, a
password plus a fingerprint, or a
password with a hardware token.
Interviewers want to know not only what
these technologies are, but why
companies use them.
>> [music]
>> The answer is simple. Single sign on
improves the user experience and MFA
improves security. Question number five,
"Walk me through the user life cycle."
This question is [music] extremely
common in IAM interviews. You should
immediately think joiners, movers, and
leavers. When a user joins, accounts are
created, assigned roles are added to
that account, and access is granted.
When a user changes roles, [music] the
permissions are updated and they remove
any unnecessary access. When a user
leaves, the account is disabled, the
access is removed, and archive data if
necessary. This process is the core of
IAM. Question six, "Tell me about a time
that you solved a technical problem."
This is where many candidates struggle.
The interviewer isn't necessarily
testing your technical knowledge,
they're evaluating how you think. Use
the STAR method: situation,
task, action, result. Even if you don't
have IAM experience yet, talk about
troubleshooting an MFA issue, solving an
Active Directory problem, automating a
task with PowerShell, and helping a user
regain access. Employers want
problem-solvers. Question seven, why do
you want to work in IAM? People don't
say, "Because cybersecurity pays well."
Talk about why IAM interests you. For
example, I enjoy the intersection of
security and business operations. IAM
plays a critical role in protecting
organizations by ensuring users have
appropriate access while maintaining
security and compliance. This question
gives employers insight into your
motivations and long-term goals. And
here's a bonus tip. Here's something
most people don't realize, you don't
need perfect answers. Interviewers care
more about how you communicate than
whether you memorize every acronym. If
you don't know an answer, stay calm,
explain your thought process, ask
clarifying questions, and show that
you're willing to learn. That mindset
will take you much farther than
memorizing every will. Let's recap on
the seven IAM interview questions that
you need to master. What is IAM?
Authentication versus authorization,
RBAC, single sign-on and MFA, the user
life cycle, and solving technical
problems. Why did you choose IAM? Master
these questions
>> [music]
>> and you'll walk into your next IAM
interview with far more confidence.
